en: The *Sūtra on the Meritorious Retribution of Carving and Erecting Images*, translated by an unknown name, appended to the Record of the Eastern Jin.
When the Buddha arrived at the kingdom of Kuru, there was a park owner named Kauśika. At that time, the kingdom...
The king’s name was Udayana; he was fourteen years of age. Hearing that the Buddha was coming, the king immediately commanded his ministers and attendants to prepare the carriage.

The king went out to welcome the Buddha; seeing the World-Honored One from afar, his heart leaped with joy and he was filled with great delight. He halted the carriage and dismounted on foot, dismissing his ministers, attendants, and those holding parasols. He then stepped forward to meet him, prostrating himself with his head to the ground in salutation. Rising again, he stepped forward once more, repeating this three times.
The Buddha said, "Come forward.
The king again approached, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, rose and circumambulated him three times, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Among all the devas in heaven and among the people on earth, none can equal the Buddha!
Now, the Buddha’s countenance, his body, and his gait—his radiance is so sublime and magnificent.”

I now gaze upon the Buddha without ever feeling weary; the Buddha is the Great Teacher of all devas and humans above and below the heavens, and the compassionate heart with which he pities and rescues is exceedingly vast.
The Buddha remained silent and did not respond.
The king spoke to the Buddha again, saying:
"For one who performs wholesome deeds, what kind of blessings and benefits will they obtain?"
"After the Buddha has departed, I fear I shall no longer behold him.
I now wish to create an image of the Buddha to pay homage and serve; what kind of meritorious retribution will I obtain?
I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will explain this for me, for I desire to hear and know it."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the young king:
"What you have asked is most excellent!
Listen attentively to my words and take them to heart."
The king then bowed his head and said,
“I accept your instruction.
The Buddha told the king:
“If there is anyone who creates an image of the Buddha, the merit and blessings thereby obtained— I shall now explain them all for you.
The King said, “Yes!”
"I accept your kindness.

The Buddha said, "Any person in the world who is able to create an image of the Buddha will, in all their future births, have pure and clean eyes and a handsome countenance; their body, hands, and feet will always be exceptionally supple and soft. Even when born in the heavens, they will be pure and superior among the gods, with eyes and facial features that are incomparably beautiful."
The merit of creating an image of the Buddha is as follows:

wherever one is born after creating an image of the Buddha, one will be free from all evils and possess a complete physical form; after death, one will attain rebirth in the seventh Brahma Heaven, and among the various devas, one’s appearance will be upright, exceptionally beautiful, and beyond compare, being revered by all the devas.
The merit of creating an image of the Buddha is as follows:

by creating an image of the Buddha, one will in future lives always be born into a family of power and noble status, receiving a physical vigor that is far superior to the world's, and wherever one is born, one shall not fall into a poor household.
The merit of creating an image of the Buddha is as follows:

"By creating an image of the Buddha, in future lives one’s physical form will be exceptionally sublime, with a lustrous purple-gold complexion and peerless beauty, always being the object of the common respect and affection of all people."
The merit of creating an image of the Buddha is such as this:

having created an image of the Buddha, one will in future lives always be born into a wealthy and noble family, with property and precious treasures beyond measure, and will always be loved and esteemed by parents, brothers, and kinsmen.
The merit of creating an image of the Buddha is such as this.
Having created an image of the Buddha, if one is later reborn within Jambudvīpa, one will always be born into the families of emperors, kings, dukes, marquises, or the virtuous and good.
The merit of creating an image of the Buddha is thus.
By creating an image of the Buddha, one will in a future life become a sovereign ruler, preeminent and superior to all other kings, and shall be venerated and looked up to by all monarchs.
The merit of creating an image of the Buddha is thus.
By creating an image of the Buddha, one will in a future life become a Cakravartin King, over whom all the kings of the four continents shall be subject.
The merit of creating an image of a Buddha is such as this:

by creating an image of a Buddha, one will in a future life become a Cakravartin King; he shall fly through the heavens and descend again at his own will, and whatever he undertakes, there is nothing he cannot accomplish.
The merit of creating an image of the Buddha is such as this:

by creating an image of the Buddha, one will be reborn in the seventh Brahma-heaven in a future life, with a lifespan of more than one kalpa, possessing supreme and unsurpassed wisdom that none can equal.
The merit of creating an image of the Buddha is such that,
when one’s lifespan in the Brahma Heaven has ended, one shall descend again to be born into a family that is filial and possesses the Way and the Dharma.
The merit of creating an image of the Buddha is such.
"By creating an image of the Buddha, one will, in future births, always be cherished and esteemed by one's parents; at the end of life, one will further attain rebirth in the heavens.
Such is the merit of creating an image of the Buddha."
“By creating an image of the Buddha, after death one will no longer fall into the three evil realms; one should guard one’s own mind and constantly seek the Buddha.

By creating an image of the Buddha, in future lives one will be held in high esteem for the sutras; with a mind desiring to always offer various fine incenses and flowers, various fine silks and banners, lamps and the light of fire, and all the famous, excellent, and precious jewels among the heavens and the world to the Buddha’s stupa, after countless kalpas, one shall surely attain the Way of the Buddha’s Nirvana.”

If there are people who, with sincere intent, offer exquisite treasures and their most cherished possessions to the Buddha, they are not ordinary persons; rather, they are all those who in previous lives fashioned images of the Buddha or practiced the path of a bodhisattva.
The merit of creating an image of the Buddha is thus.
To create an image of the Buddha brings forth immeasurable merit; it is inexhaustible and beyond calculation.

Even the rivers, seas, and waters of the four continents under heaven may still be measured in bushels; yet the merit of creating an image of the Buddha is far greater, exceeding the waters of the rivers and seas of the four continents by tenfold. In future lives, one will always protect the Buddha-way.
“Creating images of the Buddha is like this: when it rains from heaven, a person who has a fine house has nothing to fear.
By creating images of the Buddha, after death one will no longer enter the various evil realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts.”

If there are sentient beings who, upon seeing an image of the Buddha, give rise to a mind of reverence, or who join their palms in self-refuge before a Buddhist stūpa or śarīra, they shall not enter the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts for a hundred kalpas after death.

Upon death, they will be reborn in the heavens; when their lifespan there ends, they will again be born into wealthy and powerful families in the human world. Thus, they will enjoy incalculable blessings and, in due course, shall attain the path of the Buddha’s nirvana.
The Buddha told King Udayana:
"If a person performs good deeds by fashioning an image of the Buddha, the blessings, protection, and merit thereof are such that they shall never be in vain."
At that time, King Udayana praised the Buddha with these verses:
“The Buddha is the Great Sage, Who preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
In the park of Jīvaka and the Ghoṣita Garden, Udayana joined his palms and questioned him.”
"Hearing the Brahma-voice with clarity and composure, Unwavering and perfected through a hundred merits—
For one who creates an image of the Buddha, What kind of karmic reward is obtained?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
"O King, listen attentively to my words: The blessed land expands as the supreme soil;
there is no merit that surpasses this— the making of images of the Buddha.
One will always be born into a family of great wealth, possessing the most noble and boundless treasures."
One’s retinue will always show respect; this is the retribution for making images of the Buddha.
In life after life one’s body will be free from affliction; this is the retribution for [the merit of] constantly attaining the divine eye.
Possessing a peerless deep-blue complexion; this is the retribution for making images of the Buddha.
The parents see them with joyful delight; they are upright and majestic, their virtue profound.
Cherished and loved without ever weariness, they repay this by creating images of the Buddha.
Their golden bodies radiate blazing light, like the wondrous form of a lion.
Sentient beings see them and rejoice; this is the retribution for making images of the Buddha.
Among the great clans of Jambudvīpa—the Kṣatriyas and Brāhmaṇas—fortunate people are born therein;
this is the retribution for making images of the Buddha.
One shall not be born in a remote land, nor be blind or ugly;
with the six sense-faculties always complete, this is the retribution for creating images of the Buddha.
At the time of death, one will recognize one's past lives and see the Buddha standing before one.
Not perceiving the suffering at the time of death, one receives the retribution for creating images of the Buddha.
One becomes a king of great renown, a sovereign of the golden wheel who flies through the air, ruling over the four continents;
this is the retribution for creating images of the Buddha.
He acts as the cause for the name Śakra; the second is the scripture on the divine feet (*ṛddhi-pāda*).
The Thirty-three Gods offer him service, and he repays them by manifesting in the form of a Buddha.
Having transcended this realm of desire, he becomes Brahmā, the King of the Brahmā Heaven.
The assembly of Brahmās in the Kāyika heaven, out of reverence, fashioned images of the Buddha as a reward.
The merit received is exactly like this; if one can carve or paint such images, even heaven and earth might be able to weigh it, yet this merit cannot be measured.

"Therefore, by making offerings to the Buddha—offering flowers, incense, fragrant juices, and ointments—to those who make such offerings to the Great Being shall attain the unconditioned state of the exhaustion of outflows.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the King was filled with great joy; he immediately rose, went forward, and prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet. The bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, along with their five hundred ministers and attendants, all rose in joy and paid homage to the Buddha. Subsequently, they were all reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha, becoming great bodhisattvas, most honored and foremost.
When King Udayana heard what was said, he received it with joy and understanding, and immediately attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
This concludes the *Buddha-bhāṣita-pratimā-karaṇa-puṇya-vipāka-sūtra*.
